stem: A child living in a village presented with a history of drinking unpasteurized milk.
why_right: A child in a village who drinks unpasteurized milk is exposed to Brucella, a Gram negative coccobacillus spread from livestock through raw milk and dairy. Raw milk exposure is the classic stem clue for brucellosis, which presents with undulant fever, night sweats, arthralgia or back pain and hepatosplenomegaly.
why_wrong_block:
A. HSV 1: spread by saliva and close contact, not milk; presents as gingivostomatitis or cold sores, and rarely as temporal lobe encephalitis.
B. HSV 2: sexually or vertically transmitted; causes genital ulcers or neonatal herpes, nothing to do with dairy.
D. Dangue (dengue): mosquito borne (Aedes aegypti), presenting with high fever, retro-orbital pain, myalgia and thrombocytopenia; right when the stem gives travel to or residence in an endemic area with mosquito exposure.
key_concept:
Raw milk + fever = brucellosis.
  • Organism: Gram negative coccobacillus, zoonosis (goats, sheep, camels, cattle)
  • Picture: undulant fever, night sweats, arthralgia, back pain, hepatosplenomegaly
  • Initial test: serology (tube agglutination)
  • Treatment: doxycycline + rifampicin or streptomycin
  • Duration: simple 6 weeks, MSK 12 weeks, neuro 6 months
exam_pearl: Any exposure to unpasteurized milk, livestock or a veterinary job in a febrile stem should make brucellosis your first thought.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Stem lead-in not recalled. Printed 'Answer: C. Brucellosis'.

stem: A 55-year-old man with stage 2 chronic kidney disease is evaluated because of anemia. He is complaining of fatigue. His physical examination reveals pale skin, otherwise unremarkable (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to be done?
why_right: At stage 2 CKD the kidneys still make enough erythropoietin, so anemia cannot simply be blamed on the kidney; another cause, above all iron deficiency, must be looked for first. The first test in any CKD anemia is iron studies (ferritin and transferrin saturation), which separate iron deficiency from anemia of chronic disease and decide whether iron must be replaced before any ESA is considered. In a 55-year-old man, proven iron deficiency also mandates a search for GI blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
B. Reticulocyte count: useful to split a normocytic anemia into hypoproliferative vs hemolytic/blood loss, but it does not tell you whether iron stores are depleted, which is the key decision in CKD anemia.
C. Serum erythropoietin level: not routinely measured in CKD anemia because levels are uninterpretable; the diagnosis of EPO deficiency is made by excluding other causes, mainly iron deficiency.
D. Bone marrow aspiration: invasive; reserved for unexplained cytopenias or suspected marrow infiltration after the initial noninvasive workup is unrevealing.
key_concept:
CKD anemia: check iron first, treat iron first, then consider ESA.
  • First step: ferritin + TSAT
  • Low ferritin/TSAT: replace iron (and look for blood loss)
  • Iron replete + anemia persists: erythropoiesis stimulating agent
  • Early CKD (stage 1 to 2): EPO deficiency unlikely, hunt for another cause
  • Target Hb on ESA: about 10 to 11.5 g/dL, avoid above 13
exam_pearl: Early stage CKD with anemia is not 'renal anemia' until iron deficiency and other causes are excluded.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus was recently diagnosed with hypertension. Which of the following is the most appropriate antihypertensive medication?
why_right: In a patient with type 2 diabetes and newly diagnosed hypertension, an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is the first line choice regardless of age or ethnicity, because it is renoprotective: efferent arteriolar dilation lowers intraglomerular pressure and slows diabetic nephropathy. Ramipril is the only ACE inhibitor offered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hydralazine is not a first line agent for chronic hypertension; it is used for hypertension in pregnancy (IV) or as add on in resistant cases.
B. Amlodipine is first line for non diabetic patients over 55 or of African or Caribbean origin; in diabetes an ACE inhibitor comes first, and a CCB is an add on.
C. Beta blockers are not first line for uncomplicated hypertension; they are used when there is a compelling cardiac indication such as angina, post MI or heart failure.
key_concept:
Diabetes + hypertension = ACE inhibitor or ARB first.
  • Step 1, under 55 or diabetic: ACEi or ARB
  • Step 1, over 55 or African/Caribbean (non diabetic): CCB
  • Step 2: ACEi/ARB + CCB or thiazide like diuretic
  • Step 3: ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide like diuretic
  • ACEi side effects: cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia
exam_pearl: Diabetes overrides the age 55 rule: a 55+ diabetic still starts on an ACE inhibitor.

stem: A 63-year-old woman presented with exertional dyspnea for 8 months. She was diagnosed with COPD 3 years ago and has had 4 exacerbations in the last year. She completed pulmonary rehabilitation and quit smoking 2 years ago. Medications include long-acting B2 agonist, inhaled glucocorticoid, roflumilast, and albuterol as needed. Examination revealed no jugular venous distention; decreased breath sounds, a loud pulmonary component of S1 (see lab results and reports). Chest radiograph: Normal. Echocardiogram: Ejection fraction of 60%, no valvular or wall motion abnormalities, and estimated mean pulmonary artery pressure is 55 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: estimated mean pulmonary artery pressure is 55 mmHg
why_right: COPD remains uncontrolled (4 exacerbations/year) despite smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation and maximal inhaled therapy plus roflumilast. A loud pulmonary heart sound and mean PA pressure 55 mmHg with normal EF and valves mean pulmonary hypertension from lung disease, not heart disease. Long-term oxygen therapy is the treatment that improves survival and slows cor pulmonale in hypoxemic COPD, and pulmonary hypertension lowers the oxygen threshold needed to qualify.
why_wrong_block:
A. Daily prednisone: systemic steroids are for short courses in acute exacerbations; long-term daily use adds toxicity with no survival benefit.
C. Overnight pulse oximetry: a test, not a treatment; right when daytime oxygenation is adequate and isolated nocturnal desaturation is suspected.
D. Repeat pulmonary rehabilitation: she has already completed it; repeating it does not address pulmonary hypertension.
key_concept:
Survival in COPD improves with smoking cessation, long-term oxygen (if hypoxemic) and vaccination.
  • LTOT: PaO2 ≤ 55 mmHg or SaO2 ≤ 88% on room air (confirmed on repeat testing)
  • Or PaO2 56 to 59 mmHg / SaO2 89% plus pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale, edema, or polycythemia
  • Cor pulmonale: loud P2, raised JVP, edema; confirm with echo
  • Normal EF and valves exclude primary heart disease
exam_pearl: Oxygen needs documented hypoxemia: pulmonary hypertension makes a borderline PaO2 (55 to 59) enough to qualify.

stem: A 68-year-old woman known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and endstage renal disease on hemodialysis complains of shortness of breath and increasing bilateral lower limb swelling. She denies any fever, chest pain, cough, abdominal pain, or vomiting. Examination reveals an ill-looking patient with high JVP and +3 lower limb edema. ECG was ordered (see lab result). Which of the following is the most likely ECG finding?
why_right: An ESRD patient on hemodialysis who is volume overloaded (high JVP, +3 edema) suggests missed or inadequate dialysis, and the accompanying labs show hyperkalemia. The earliest classic ECG sign of hyperkalemia is a tall, peaked T wave, so this is the most likely finding.
why_wrong_block:
B. Peaked P wave: P pulmonale of right atrial enlargement; in hyperkalemia the P wave flattens and then disappears.
C. Short PR interval: suggests pre-excitation such as WPW; hyperkalemia prolongs the PR interval.
D. Narrow QRS complex: hyperkalemia widens the QRS as it worsens, it never narrows it.
key_concept:
Hyperkalemia ECG progression (worsens as K rises):
  • Peaked T waves (earliest)
  • PR prolongation, flattened then absent P waves
  • QRS widening
  • Sine wave pattern, then VF or asystole
  • Hypokalemia, by contrast: flat T waves and U waves
exam_pearl: Dialysis patient + missed session (overload) = think hyperkalemia first; peaked T, not peaked P.

stem: A 69-year-old man is diagnosed recently with lymphoma and started on chemotherapy. On day 7 post 4th cycle, he presented to the Emergency Room with fever. Examination precludes any underlying infection (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
OptC: Blood culture and wait for sensitivity
OptD: Empiric IV antibiotics in a hospital setting
why_right: A lymphoma patient on chemotherapy with fever on "day 7 post 4th cycle" is at the expected neutrophil nadir, so fever without a source is treated as febrile neutropenia, a medical emergency. Take cultures (septic screen) and start empiric broad spectrum IV antibiotics in hospital immediately. His age (69) makes him high risk, so he is admitted rather than managed as an outpatient.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antifungals are not first line; they are added only when fever persists for several days despite broad spectrum antibiotics. NSAIDs mask fever and impair platelet function in a patient who may also be thrombocytopenic.
B. Oral antibiotics at home are reserved for carefully selected low risk patients; an elderly patient at the chemotherapy nadir needs admission and IV therapy.
C. Cultures are taken, but waiting for sensitivities delays treatment of a potentially rapidly fatal infection; antibiotics are started empirically right after cultures.
key_concept:
Fever in a patient on chemotherapy = febrile neutropenia until proven otherwise.
  • Nadir: about 7 to 14 days after a cycle
  • Step 1: full septic screen (blood cultures, urine, CXR as indicated)
  • Step 2: empiric broad spectrum IV antibiotics without waiting for results
  • Persistent fever after several days of antibiotics: add antifungal
  • Outpatient oral therapy: only for selected low risk patients
exam_pearl: Do not wait for the neutrophil count or culture results; a source does not need to be found to start IV antibiotics.

stem: A 70-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-hour history of confusion and irritability. He was well until 5 days ago, when he injured his right leg and has been bed-bound since the accident. He is hypertensive and wellcontrolled on medication. He has no fever (see reports). Chest X-ray: Normal. ECG: Sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: injured his right leg and has been bed-bound
why_right: Injured leg and "bed-bound" for 5 days is a major DVT/PE risk factor. Sudden "confusion and irritability" in an elderly patient reflects hypoxemia, "no fever" argues against infection, and a "normal" chest X-ray with "sinus tachycardia" (the commonest ECG finding in PE) is the typical PE picture.
why_wrong_block:
A. The ECG shows sinus rhythm; an arrhythmia would be the answer if it showed AF, VT or a block causing low output.
B. Cerebral infarction gives focal deficits (weakness, aphasia, facial droop), not isolated confusion with tachycardia; immobility is not its key risk factor.
C. Brain hemorrhage presents with sudden headache, focal signs or reduced consciousness, often with uncontrolled hypertension; his BP is well controlled.
key_concept:
Suspect PE with risk factor + unexplained tachycardia or hypoxia.
  • Risks: immobilization, recent surgery or trauma, long travel, OCP, malignancy
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia most common; S1Q3T3 and RBBB are classic
  • CXR is usually normal
  • Gold standard: CT pulmonary angiography
  • V/Q scan if CT contraindicated or inconclusive
  • Elderly may present with confusion only
exam_pearl: Normal chest X-ray with sinus tachycardia and a risk factor: PE, not a lung disease.

stem: A 19-year-old male with known hepatitis B presents with bilateral knee pain for 2 days and has been extensively taking paracetamol. Serology: HBsAb: negative HBsAg: positive HBeAg: negative HBc IgG: positive Lab: AST over 2000 ALT were over 1000, Bilirubin 27 ( normal 5.1 – 17.0 mmol/L) INR was 2.something What is the Most appropriate treatment
OptC: Entecavir to treat acute hepatitis B
why_right: He has been taking paracetamol extensively for knee pain and now has AST over 2000, ALT over 1000, raised bilirubin and an INR above 2: acute hepatocellular injury with failing synthetic function, typical of paracetamol hepatotoxicity. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is given in any paracetamol liver injury, including staggered or repeated supratherapeutic intake where the nomogram cannot be used. His serology (HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgG positive, HBeAg negative) is background chronic hepatitis B, not the cause of this acute rise.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV corticosteroid: used for autoimmune hepatitis or severe alcoholic hepatitis; no role in paracetamol injury, and steroids can trigger a flare of hepatitis B.
C. Entecavir to treat acute hepatitis B: the serology is chronic (anti-HBc IgG, no acute markers), not acute HBV, and an antiviral does not treat drug toxicity. Right for chronic HBV with raised transaminases or active disease.
D. Plasmapheresis with penicillamine: Wilson disease therapy (copper chelation, plasmapheresis as a bridge in acute Wilsonian liver failure); right with low ceruloplasmin, Kayser Fleischer rings and Coombs negative hemolysis.
key_concept:
Paracetamol + raised transaminases = give NAC now; do not wait for a level.
  • Single acute ingestion with known time: plot level on the nomogram
  • Staggered or repeated excess use: nomogram invalid, treat if LFTs raised or level detectable
  • Markedly raised AST/ALT + rising INR = hepatotoxicity, consider liver unit referral
  • HBsAg+ / anti-HBc IgG+ = chronic HBV
  • Sudden acute hepatitis in a chronic HBV carrier without a drug cause: think HDV superinfection
exam_pearl: A known liver disease in the stem is often a distractor: the drug history (excess paracetamol) explains the acute picture.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed short version: 'About pt known case of chronic HepB c/o fatigue, LOC and jaundice for 2 days used paracetamol in excessive amount for his knee pain, have high liver enzyme .. long long scenario High ALT AST INR 2 Most appropriate mx?' with B. Acetylcysteine highlighted. Fuller version ends with 'Answer: B. N- Acetylcysteine'.

stem: Typical case of brucellosis ( arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly back pain hx of drink unpasteurized milk) no neurological symptoms no labs no imaging What is the recommended duration of treatment?
why_right: The stem stresses a typical case with no neurological symptoms and no imaging showing focal disease, so this is simple (uncomplicated) brucellosis. Simple brucellosis is treated with doxycycline plus rifampicin or streptomycin for 6 weeks; longer courses are reserved for proven focal complications.
why_wrong_block:
A. 3 weeks: too short for any form of brucellosis and associated with relapse.
C. 12 weeks: the duration for musculoskeletal brucellosis with spondylitis or sacroiliitis confirmed on imaging; right when the stem gives MRI or X-ray evidence of spinal or sacroiliac involvement.
D. 21 weeks: not a standard brucellosis duration; the longest standard course is about 6 months, for neurobrucellosis.
key_concept:
Brucellosis duration depends on the site.
  • Simple: 6 weeks
  • Musculoskeletal (spondylitis, sacroiliitis): 12 weeks
  • Neurobrucellosis: 6 months
  • Regimen: doxycycline + rifampicin or streptomycin
exam_pearl: Back pain alone does not make it MSK brucellosis; the 12 week course needs imaging proven spondylitis or sacroiliitis.

stem: female admitted for mycoplasma pneumonia was started on antibiotics and supportive therapy. On day 3 she developed yellowish discoloration of the eyes and mild abdominal pain. Labs: Hb 68 g/L (low) Reticulocytes 4% (elevated) Haptoglobin low LDH high normal ALT high AST. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: The labs show hemolysis: Hb 68 with raised reticulocytes, low haptoglobin, high LDH and a high AST with normal ALT (AST released from red cells), plus jaundice. This recall's key is to stop antibiotics, reading the onset on day 3 after starting antibiotics as drug induced immune hemolytic anemia, which is treated by withdrawing the culprit drug. The source itself is debated, because Mycoplasma infection is also a classic cause of cold agglutinin hemolysis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observe: right when the hemolysis is Mycoplasma related cold agglutinin (IgM) hemolysis, which is usually self limited and managed supportively (keep warm, transfuse if severe) while the infection is treated.
C. Corticosteroids: first line for warm (IgG) autoimmune hemolytic anemia, e.g. with SLE or CLL; they work poorly in cold agglutinin hemolysis and are not needed once a drug cause is removed.
D. Oral Rituximab: rituximab is given intravenously, not orally, and is reserved for chronic primary cold agglutinin disease or steroid refractory warm AIHA, not an acute infection related episode.
key_concept:
Confirm hemolysis, then find the trigger.
  • Hemolysis: low Hb, high retics, low haptoglobin, high LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, AST > ALT
  • Direct Coombs: IgG = warm AIHA or drug; C3 only = cold agglutinin
  • Drug induced: stop the drug (e.g. ceftriaxone, penicillins)
  • Mycoplasma / EBV: IgM cold agglutinins, supportive care, keep warm
  • Warm AIHA: steroids first, rituximab if refractory
exam_pearl: New hemolysis days after starting a drug points to the drug; Mycoplasma cold agglutinins typically appear later in the illness.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Typed option D reads 'Oral Rituximab answer' but the compiler highlights B. A fuller 'Q:' version (30 year-old female, Hb 60, retics high, LDH elevated, haptoglobin 0.3 low, PLT/WBC/LFT normal; options Observe / Stop antibiotics / start corticosteroids / start rituximab) also highlights B. Stop antibiotics.
Other marked answers: Typed option label: D. Oral Rituximab ('answer' written after it)

stem: A 70-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with generalized fatigability. Two days ago, he underwent a contrast-enhanced CT brain scan for suspected transient ischemic attack. Physical examination is unremarkable. Vital signs show blood pressure of 130/70 mmHg and heart rate of 76/min. Laboratory investigations reveal: Hb: 170 g/L (normal) Urea: 30.4 mmol/L (elevated) Creatinine: 378 µmol/L (elevated) What is the most likely mechanism for the renal impairment?
why_right: Creatinine has risen to 378 with high urea two days after a contrast enhanced CT, in a 70 year old with normal blood pressure and heart rate and an unremarkable exam. AKI within 48 to 72 hours of iodinated contrast is contrast induced nephropathy, whose mechanism is acute tubular necrosis from renal vasoconstriction and direct tubular toxicity.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pre-renal azotemia: needs hypovolemia or poor perfusion (postural hypotension, tachycardia, concentrated urine with low FeNa); vitals here are normal. Right in dehydration, e.g. a recruit after excessive training.
C. Acute interstitial nephritis: a hypersensitivity reaction to drugs such as beta lactams or NSAIDs, with fever, rash and eosinophiluria; contrast nephropathy does not work this way.
D. Acute glomerular nephritis: expect hematuria with RBC casts, edema, hypertension or a recent infection; contrast does not cause GN.
key_concept:
AKI after contrast = ATN.
  • Timing: creatinine rises within 48 to 72 hours of contrast
  • Urine: muddy brown granular casts
  • Pre-renal: hypovolemia, urine osmolality high, FeNa below 1%
  • AIN: drug + fever, rash, eosinophiluria
  • Prevention: hydration before and after contrast, monitor renal function
exam_pearl: Normal vitals rule out the pre-renal trap; recent contrast plus rising creatinine is ATN.

stem: Woman with diarrhea and they said on examination she seems dehydrated. She visited her clinic last week; creatinine was 60. Now presenting with: Plasma Creatinine: 160 BUN: 11 Na: 133 Urine: Urine sodium: 60 Osmolality: 220
why_right: Creatinine rose from 60 to 160 within a week, so this is acute kidney injury. Diarrhea and dehydration started it, but the urine now shows urine sodium 60 and osmolality 220: the tubules can no longer hold on to sodium or concentrate urine. That intrinsic pattern means prolonged prerenal hypoperfusion has progressed to acute tubular necrosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Prerenal: the tubules still work, so urine sodium is low (<20) and urine is concentrated (osmolality >500). Here sodium is 60 and osmolality 220, the opposite pattern. It would be correct with the same history but low urine sodium and concentrated urine.
C. Acute on chronic kidney disease: this needs an abnormal baseline. Her creatinine was a normal 60 last week, so there is no chronic disease underneath.
key_concept:
Urine indices separate prerenal AKI (working tubules) from ATN (damaged tubules).
  • Urine Na: prerenal <20; ATN >40
  • FeNa: prerenal <1%; ATN >2%
  • Urine osmolality: prerenal >500; ATN <300 (isosthenuric)
  • Specific gravity: prerenal >1.020; ATN ≈1.010
  • Sediment: prerenal bland; ATN muddy brown granular casts
  • If dehydration persists, prerenal AKI turns into ischemic ATN
exam_pearl: A dehydration history does not make it prerenal. Read the urine: high urine Na with dilute urine means ATN.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered recall placed under 972; answer line reads 'A. Acute tubular necrosis'.

stem: 30 years old male , on vit d supplements because he had deficiency , polyurea , polydipsia , normal urine osmolality , slightly high pth , very low c peptide , family hx of dm, niece with dm type 1 , what's the diagnosis :
why_right: Polyuria and polydipsia with a very low C peptide mean the body is making almost no insulin. Beta cell failure is the defining feature of type 1 diabetes, and a relative with type 1 fits too. Onset at 30 is still possible: autoimmune diabetes can present in adults, including the slower form called LADA.
why_wrong_block:
B. Type 2: insulin resistance with normal or high C peptide, at least early on. It would be correct in an obese adult with a preserved C peptide.
C. Diabetes insipidus: polyuria with very dilute urine (low urine osmolality) and high serum sodium or osmolality. Here urine osmolality is normal, so DI is unlikely.
D. Hyperparathyroidism: a slightly high PTH in someone being treated for vitamin D deficiency is secondary hyperparathyroidism, a physiological response. Primary disease needs high calcium with high PTH.
key_concept:
C peptide tells you whether the pancreas is still making insulin.
  • Low or undetectable C peptide: type 1 (or late-stage insulin deficiency)
  • Normal or high C peptide: type 2 (insulin resistance)
  • Polyuria with dilute urine and high serum osmolality: diabetes insipidus
  • Low vitamin D with mildly high PTH and low or normal calcium: secondary hyperparathyroidism
  • High calcium with high PTH: primary hyperparathyroidism
exam_pearl: Do not rule out type 1 because the patient is 30. Very low C peptide decides it, whatever the age.

stem: Female in 40s with murmur (forgot the murmur description) and High BP; the question asks what is most important preventive measure. Options:
why_right: This recall's key is an echocardiogram. A new murmur in a hypertensive woman in her 40s has to be characterised (valve lesion, LV hypertrophy, function) before any later decisions, such as endocarditis prophylaxis or follow-up, can be made. The other two options are a wrong screening interval and prophylaxis she does not qualify for.
why_wrong_block:
B. Annual flexible sigmoidoscopy: the interval is wrong. Flexible sigmoidoscopy screening is every 5 years (colonoscopy every 10), starting at 45 for average risk. It also does nothing about the cardiac finding.
C. Antibiotic before dental procedures: this is reserved for high-risk cardiac patients only (prosthetic valve, previous endocarditis, certain cyanotic congenital heart disease, transplant with valvulopathy). An uncharacterised native-valve murmur does not qualify.
key_concept:
Endocarditis prophylaxis depends on the patient's risk, not on whether a murmur is present.
  • Give it (amoxicillin) only for high-risk cardiac conditions undergoing high-risk procedures such as tooth extraction
  • High risk: prosthetic valve, previous endocarditis, unrepaired or recently repaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, transplant valvulopathy
  • Native valve disease or murmur alone: no prophylaxis
  • New or unexplained murmur: echocardiography
  • Colorectal screening from 45: colonoscopy every 10 years, flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5, FIT yearly
exam_pearl: Murmur plus dental visit is the trap. A native-valve murmur alone never earns antibiotic prophylaxis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Stem partly in Arabic (recaller forgot the murmur characteristics).

stem: 38 years old female patient known diagnosed of ulcerative colitis 6 or 8 yaers ago, she is on maintenance therapy came to PHC for follow up and asking when she do colonoscopy, only complain for her is PERIanal pain, otherwise normal
OptA: now as she has perianal pain
OptC: 8-10 years after diagnosis of ulcerative colitis
why_right: Ulcerative colitis raises colorectal cancer risk according to how long and how extensive the colitis has been, not according to the patient's age. Surveillance colonoscopy therefore starts about 8 to 10 years after diagnosis (symptom onset), then repeats every 1 to 3 years depending on risk. Her colitis began 6 to 8 years ago, so she is entering that window.
why_wrong_block:
A. Now because of perianal pain: perianal pain points to a local problem such as a fissure, hemorrhoid or abscess, or raises the question of Crohn's. It calls for an examination, not cancer surveillance colonoscopy.
B. At 50, then every 10 years: that is average-risk population screening (now from 45). UC patients are high risk, so they start earlier and are scoped more often.
key_concept:
Colitis-associated cancer surveillance runs on a different clock from population screening.
  • UC or Crohn's colitis: first colonoscopy 8 to 10 years after symptom onset
  • Then every 1 to 3 years by risk (extent, inflammation, dysplasia, family history)
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis with colitis: surveillance from diagnosis, then yearly
  • Average risk: from 45, colonoscopy every 10 years
exam_pearl: In IBD, count the years since diagnosis, not the patient's age. PSC starts the clock immediately.

stem: A 63-year-old man is evaluated for hemoptysis and a 5-kg weight loss over the last 2 months. He has a history of 30 pack-years of smoking but stopped 10 days ago (see reports). Chest X-ray: 5-cm irregular mass in the right upper lobe. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy: Tumor in the right upper lobe bronchus. Biopsy: Squamous cell carcinoma. Whole body FDG-PET scan: Negative for metastasis. Which of the following is the most appropriate action while preparing him for surgery?
why_right: He has a 5 cm squamous cell carcinoma with a PET negative for metastasis, so the plan is curative resection. Before any lung resection, pulmonary function tests (FEV1 and DLCO) are required to confirm he has enough reserve to tolerate removal of lung tissue and to provide a baseline.
why_wrong_block:
A. Repeating PET in 3 months would delay curative surgery for a proven cancer; PET is already negative for metastasis. Any further staging would be mediastinal node sampling now, not a delayed repeat scan.
C. Chemotherapy does not answer 'preparing him for surgery'. Neoadjuvant or adjuvant systemic therapy is an oncology decision based on stage and pathology, and fitness (PFT) must be confirmed whatever is decided.
D. Radiotherapy is for patients unfit for surgery or for palliation. This patient is being prepared for resection.
key_concept:
Before lung cancer resection: confirm stage, then confirm fitness.
  • Staging: CT chest/abdomen, PET/CT, mediastinal sampling if nodes suspicious
  • Fitness: PFTs (FEV1, DLCO)
  • Low predicted post-op values: exercise testing
  • Smoking cessation before surgery
  • Unfit for surgery: stereotactic or radical radiotherapy
exam_pearl: Lead-in says 'while preparing for surgery': the answer is a fitness test, not more oncologic treatment.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall highlights B; accompanying screenshot (0038) also 'Answer: B'.

stem: A 50-year-old man is 6 days post-uneventful subtotal colectomy and ileocolic anastomosis when he develops sudden-onset shortness of breath and one episode of hemoptysis. Examination reveals mildly decreased breath sounds at the left lung base, normal S1 and S2, a soft and lax abdomen with normal bowel sounds, and no lower extremities edema or tenderness (see lab results and reports). Chest X-ray: Left basilar atelectasis. ECG: Sinus tachycardia and a new finding of a right bundle branch block. Which of the following is the most appropriate test?
highlight_terms_source: new finding of a right bundle branch block
why_right: Day 6 after major abdominal surgery, sudden dyspnea, hemoptysis, sinus tachycardia and a new RBBB (right heart strain) make the pretest probability of PE high. In a high-probability patient you go straight to the definitive test, CT pulmonary angiography, which is the gold standard for PE.
why_wrong_block:
A. D-dimer is only useful to rule out PE in LOW probability patients; after recent surgery it is almost always raised, so it adds nothing here.
B. Bedside echocardiography is used when the patient is hemodynamically UNSTABLE (shock, hypotension) and cannot go to CT, to look for RV strain. No shock is described here, and echo cannot confirm PE.
D. Leg Doppler finds DVT but he has no leg swelling or tenderness, and a negative result would not exclude PE. It is the first test in pregnancy or when CTPA is contraindicated.
key_concept:
Suspected PE: choose the test by probability and stability.
  • Low probability: D-dimer (negative excludes)
  • High probability, stable: CTPA
  • Unstable: bedside echo, consider thrombolysis
  • Pregnancy: leg ultrasound first
  • Contrast allergy or renal failure: V/Q scan
exam_pearl: Postoperative patient: D-dimer is useless because surgery alone raises it.

stem: 65-year-old woman with long-standing chronic renal failure presents with aches and pains for 1 month. Physical examination is unremarkable apart from general pallor (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: In long-standing chronic renal failure, the kidney cannot perform 1-alpha hydroxylation, so active vitamin D is deficient, causing hypocalcemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy. Aches and pains (bone pain) are the result. Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is already active and bypasses the failed renal step.
why_wrong_block:
B. Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) is an inactive precursor needing renal activation; right for nutritional deficiency or rickets with normal kidneys.
C. Vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol) is also an inactive precursor dependent on renal 1-alpha hydroxylase, so it fails to correct the deficit in advanced CKD.
D. Calcitonin nasal spray is for acute osteoporotic vertebral fracture pain or (parenterally) hypercalcemia; it does nothing for CKD mineral bone disease.
key_concept:
CKD bone disease: kidney fails to activate vitamin D and to excrete phosphate.
  • Labs: low Ca, high phosphate, high PTH, low 1,25 vitamin D
  • Give active vitamin D: calcitriol (or alfacalcidol)
  • Control phosphate: diet and phosphate binders
  • Normal kidneys + nutritional deficiency: D3 or D2
exam_pearl: The deciding word is 'renal': with failed kidneys, only the already-activated form (calcitriol) works.

stem: A 69-year-old man known to have diabetes mellitus, presented to Emergency department with 4-day history of productive cough and tachypnea. On examination, oriented to time place and person. Chest exam revealed right lower lobe crepitation (see lab results and report). Respiratory rate 23 /min Temperature 38.5 °C WBC 12 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Urea 5 2.75-7.4 mmol/L Chest X-Ray: Right lower lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most appropriate management approach?
OptA: Admit to general ward and start IV antibiotics
OptB: Admit to Intensive care unit and start IV antibiotics
OptC: Start oral antibiotics and observe in Emergency Room for 24 hours
OptD: Start oral antibiotics and see in outpatient clinic in 7-days
highlight_terms_source: oriented to time place and person
why_right: This recall's key is ward admission with IV antibiotics. The reasoning: a 69-year-old diabetic with confirmed right lower lobe pneumonia, fever 38.5, tachypnea (RR 23) and leukocytosis has age and comorbidity that raise his risk. He is oriented, urea is normal and nothing suggests shock or respiratory failure, so the ICU is not needed.
why_wrong_block:
B. ICU: for severe pneumonia (CURB-65 3 to 5, septic shock needing vasopressors, respiratory failure needing ventilation). He is oriented with RR 23 and normal urea.
C. Oral antibiotics with 24 hours of ER observation: this is not a standard disposition. Patients are either treated as outpatients or admitted.
D. Oral antibiotics with clinic review in 7 days: suits a CURB-65 0 to 1 patient who is otherwise well. Even then, review should be at 48 to 72 hours, not 7 days.
key_concept:
CURB-65 decides where community-acquired pneumonia is treated.
  • C confusion, U urea >7, R RR ≥30, B SBP <90 or DBP ≤60, age ≥65: 1 point each
  • 0 to 1: consider home treatment
  • 2: admit to ward or arrange close outpatient follow-up
  • 3 to 5: severe, admit and consider ICU
  • Hypoxia, multilobar disease, frailty or inability to take oral drugs push toward admission
exam_pearl: Score CURB-65 before choosing where to treat. Age alone gives 1 point, and hypoxia overrides the score.

stem: A 50-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease. presents to the Nephrology Clinic for follow-up (see image and lab results). Blood pressure 160/98 mmHg Heart rate 80 /min Test Result Normal Values Potassium 6.5 3.5-5.1 mmol/L Creatinine 440 44- 115 mol/L. ECG: peaked T waves. Which of the following is the best immediate step in management?
why_right: Potassium 6.5 with peaked T waves means hyperkalemia is already affecting the heart. The best immediate step is IV calcium gluconate, which stabilises the myocardial membrane within minutes and protects against arrhythmia. It does not lower potassium; shifting and removal come after.
why_wrong_block:
B. IV sodium bicarbonate: shifts potassium into cells, mainly when there is metabolic acidosis. It is an adjunct and does not protect the heart first.
C. Insulin with dextrose: the main shifting step, given right after calcium. It is the first drug when potassium is high but the ECG is normal.
D. Dialysis: removes potassium definitively in CKD or refractory hyperkalemia, but it takes time to arrange. It comes after the membrane is stabilised and potassium is shifted.
key_concept:
Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is treated in a fixed order: protect, shift, remove.
  • 1. Protect: IV calcium gluconate (ECG changes)
  • 2. Shift: insulin with dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate if acidotic
  • 3. Remove: loop diuretic, cation exchange resin, dialysis
  • No ECG changes: start with insulin with dextrose
exam_pearl: Any ECG change, even just peaked T waves, means calcium comes first. A normal ECG means insulin with dextrose comes first.

stem: A 61-year-old obese man presented with daytime somnolence, poor concentration, nocturia, and progressive shortness of breath. Examination reveals an obese patient with bilateral lower limb edema and normal vesicular breath sounds on lung auscultation. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
why_right: An "obese" man with "daytime somnolence, poor concentration, nocturia" is classic obstructive sleep apnea. Leg edema and dyspnea with "normal vesicular breath sounds" point to OSA complicated by pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale, not a primary lung disease. The test that establishes OSA is a sleep study (polysomnography).
why_wrong_block:
A. Chest X-ray cannot diagnose a sleep-related breathing disorder; it is the first test for pneumonia, effusion or pneumothorax, and the lungs are clinically normal here.
C. Echocardiography shows consequences (pulmonary hypertension, right heart strain) but not the cause; it is the answer when heart failure or valve disease is the suspected diagnosis.
D. HRCT is for interstitial lung disease (Velcro crackles, clubbing); breath sounds here are normal.
key_concept:
Obesity + daytime sleepiness = OSA until proven otherwise; diagnose with polysomnography.
  • Features: snoring, witnessed apneas, choking at night, somnolence, nocturia, morning headache
  • Complications: hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale
  • Diagnosis: sleep study (polysomnography)
  • Initial treatment: weight loss
  • Most effective treatment: CPAP
exam_pearl: Edema and dyspnea tempt you to echo, but "establish the diagnosis" asks for the underlying cause: sleep study.

stem: A patient with highly suspicious pulmonary tuberculosis is evaluated in the Emergency Department. Standard universal precautions are taken. Which of the following is the most appropriate infection control precaution during the assessment?
why_right: "Highly suspicious pulmonary tuberculosis" spreads by airborne droplet nuclei that stay suspended in air, so airborne precautions are added to the standard precautions already in place: N95 respirator and a single negative pressure room.
why_wrong_block:
A. Standard precautions alone: apply to every patient but do not protect against airborne spread.
B. Standard and droplet: for large-droplet spread within about a metre (influenza, meningococcus, pertussis, mycoplasma), where a surgical mask suffices; TB nuclei stay airborne and need an N95.
C. Standard and contact: for organisms spread by touch (MRSA, C. difficile, scabies).
key_concept:
Transmission-based precautions are added on top of standard precautions.
  • Airborne (N95, negative pressure room): TB, measles, varicella
  • Droplet (surgical mask): influenza, meningococcus, pertussis, mumps, mycoplasma
  • Contact (gown, gloves): MRSA, C. difficile, scabies
  • Typical bacterial pneumonia: standard precautions only
exam_pearl: Suspected pulmonary TB, measles or chickenpox = airborne (N95 + negative pressure room); a surgical mask (droplet) is not enough.

stem: A 17-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with severe asthma exacerbation that began 12 hours ago. He is on an albuterol inhaler and a long-acting glucocorticoid at home without improvement. He was hospitalized and intubated 2 years ago. Examination revealed respiratory distress with diffuse expiratory wheezes. After 1 hour of systemic glucocorticoid and B2 agonist nebulizer, he still appeared in respiratory distress (see lab results and report). Chest X-ray: Hyperinflated lungs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptC: Admit to the general medical floor
OptD: Discharge home the next day with follow-up
why_right: He has a severe exacerbation, a history of "intubation 2 years ago", and remains in respiratory distress "after 1 hour" of systemic glucocorticoid and nebulized beta-2 agonist. Prior intubation marks him as high risk for fatal asthma, and failure to respond to initial therapy means he may deteriorate to respiratory failure. He needs ICU admission for close monitoring and escalation (e.g. IV magnesium, possible ventilation).
why_wrong_block:
B. Discharge home is only for patients who respond well to initial treatment and have no distress; he is still in respiratory distress.
C. A general medical ward suits patients with a partial response and no high-risk features; prior intubation and persistent distress require ICU-level care.
D. Discharge with follow-up is for good responders with stable observations; it is unsafe in an unresponsive, high-risk patient.
key_concept:
Acute asthma disposition depends on response to the first hour of treatment and risk history.
  • Sequence: oxygen, SABA, ipratropium, systemic steroid, reassess
  • Good response: discharge with ICS and follow-up
  • Partial response, no high-risk features: ward admission
  • Poor response, prior intubation/ICU, rising PaCO2, drowsiness, silent chest: ICU
  • IV magnesium is the last drug step before intubation
exam_pearl: Prior intubation plus no improvement after 1 hour of treatment means ICU, not the ward.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0292).

stem: A 30-year-old woman is evaluated for new-onset nonproductive cough and dyspnea on exertion. She is pregnant at 30 weeks gestation. Medical history is unremarkable. Her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. She has a gravid uterus and 2+ edema of the lower extremities without calf tenderness. Doppler ultrasonography of both legs is negative for deep venous thrombosis (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to perform next?
highlight_terms_source: Doppler ultrasonography of both legs is negative
why_right: New dyspnea and cough at 30 weeks raise suspicion of pulmonary embolism. The first test in pregnancy, bilateral leg Doppler, has already come back negative for DVT, so the work-up moves on to lung imaging. When the chest X-ray is normal (expected with her normal cardiopulmonary exam), a V/Q scan is preferred because it gives less radiation to maternal breast tissue than CT angiography.
why_wrong_block:
A. D-dimer: it rises normally through pregnancy, so it is unreliable and cannot exclude PE. It is useful in non-pregnant patients with low pretest probability.
B. CT angiography: an acceptable alternative, chosen when the chest X-ray is abnormal or V/Q is unavailable or non-diagnostic. With a normal chest X-ray, V/Q is the preferred next test in pregnancy.
C. Pulmonary function test: assesses airway or restrictive disease such as asthma. It does not diagnose PE and would delay the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Suspected PE in pregnancy has its own ladder.
  • Step 1: bilateral compression ultrasound of the legs; if DVT is found, anticoagulate with no further imaging
  • Step 2 (ultrasound negative): chest X-ray; if normal, V/Q scan; if abnormal, CT pulmonary angiography
  • Normal V/Q: PE excluded; high probability: treat; non-diagnostic: CTPA
  • D-dimer is unreliable in pregnancy
  • Treatment is LMWH (warfarin is teratogenic)
exam_pearl: In pregnancy, a negative leg Doppler with a normal chest X-ray leads to a V/Q scan, not a D-dimer.

stem: A 48-year-old woman is evaluated for persistent fever and flank pain. She was admitted several days ago for treatment of pyelonephritis. Her fever is persistent after 5 days of starting an appropriate antibiotic. Examination reveals tenderness over the left loin area, otherwise unremarkable (see report). Urine culture: Positive for Escherichia coli susceptible to the antibiotic that was already started. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: after 5 days of starting an appropriate antibiotic
why_right: Her fever persists after 5 days of an antibiotic to which the E. coli is susceptible, with ongoing left loin tenderness. When pyelonephritis fails to respond to correct therapy, the problem is structural, not microbial: obstruction (obstructive uropathy) or a renal or perinephric abscess. Kidney ultrasound is the next step to find a lesion that may need drainage.
why_wrong_block:
B. The culture proves the organism is susceptible to the current antibiotic, so resistance is not the explanation; change antibiotics only when sensitivities show resistance.
C. A culture with sensitivities is already available; repeating it will not reveal obstruction or an abscess.
D. Fever for 5 days on appropriate therapy is treatment failure; observing risks missing an abscess or infected obstructed kidney needing drainage.
key_concept:
Pyelonephritis not improving
  • No response after 48 to 72 h of appropriate antibiotic = image the kidneys
  • Ultrasound (or CT) looks for obstruction, renal or perinephric abscess
  • Resistant organism on culture = change antibiotic
  • Obstructed infected kidney = urgent drainage
exam_pearl: Susceptible organism + persistent fever = look for pus or obstruction (image), not a new antibiotic.

stem: A 60-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is on insulin lispro (rapid-acting) and glargine (longacting). He works out after lunch and recently experienced hypoglycemia after exercise. What is the best way to prevent postexercise hypoglycemia?
OptA: Eat more carbohydrates before the workout
OptB: Change both insulins to a sulfonylurea
why_right: This recall's key is extra carbohydrate before the workout. Exercise increases glucose uptake by muscle, and with lunchtime lispro still acting this produces post-exercise hypoglycemia. Taking more carbohydrate before exercising offsets that extra glucose use while keeping his basal-bolus regimen intact.
why_wrong_block:
B. Switch to a sulfonylurea: sulfonylureas need working beta cells. In type 1 diabetes there are none, so this would cause severe hyperglycemia and DKA. Sulfonylureas also cause hypoglycemia themselves.
C. Skip lispro: omitting the meal bolus entirely leaves the lunch carbohydrate uncovered and risks hyperglycemia. The accepted adjustment is to reduce the pre-exercise prandial dose, not skip it.
D. Glargine in the morning: changing basal timing is for fasting or nocturnal hypoglycemia. His problem is tied to exercise after a prandial dose, so the basal dose is not the cause.
key_concept:
Match the insulin change to when the hypoglycemia happens.
  • Exercise-related lows: reduce the pre-exercise prandial (rapid-acting) dose and/or take extra carbohydrate
  • Fasting or nocturnal lows: reduce basal insulin (glargine)
  • Both fasting and postprandial lows: reduce both
  • Type 1 diabetes always needs insulin; oral secretagogues do not work
exam_pearl: Exercise lows point to the prandial insulin or carbohydrate intake, not the basal insulin. A sulfonylurea is never an option in type 1.

stem: SLE patient on drugs Low haptoglopin 0.2 High LDH 1200 What type of anemia
OptA: IDA ( iron and ferritin were normal in labs )
why_right: Low haptoglobin (0.2) means free hemoglobin is being cleared after red cells break down, and LDH 1200 is released from the destroyed cells. Together they are the signature of hemolysis. SLE is a classic cause of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Coombs positive), and some of her drugs could also cause hemolysis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Iron deficiency: microcytic, with low ferritin and high TIBC. The card says iron and ferritin are normal, and IDA does not lower haptoglobin.
B. Anemia of chronic disease: common in SLE, but it is a hypoproliferative anemia with normal or high ferritin. It does not cause low haptoglobin or a marked LDH rise.
C. Pernicious anemia: macrocytic with low B12 and neurological signs. Intramedullary destruction of megaloblasts can raise LDH and even lower haptoglobin, but in SLE with iron studies normal the expected cause is autoimmune hemolysis. Choose it when the MCV is high and B12 is low.
key_concept:
Hemolysis markers: low haptoglobin, high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, high reticulocytes.
  • SLE: warm AIHA, so check the direct Coombs test
  • IDA: low ferritin, high TIBC, microcytic
  • Anemia of chronic disease: normal or high ferritin, low TIBC
  • B12 deficiency: high MCV, hypersegmented neutrophils, neurological signs
exam_pearl: Low haptoglobin plus high LDH in SLE means hemolysis; megaloblastic anemia can mimic these markers but needs a high MCV and low B12.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthris who maintained on methotrexate 15 mg weekly. She iscurrently on remission. 4 months ago, her liver fune on tests were normal but the most recent liver function tests are shown (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Aspartate aminotransferase 300 12-40 10/L Alanine aminotransferase 280 5-40 IU/L Albumin 30 34-56 g/L What is the most appropriate ac on to be done for her abnormal liver fune Don tests?
why_right: Her LFTs were normal 4 months ago and now AST 300 and ALT 280 are more than 3 times the upper limit while she takes methotrexate. That points to drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Methotrexate is stopped (withheld) at once to prevent progression to fibrosis, and since her RA is in remission she can afford a pause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver ultrasound: may be part of a later work-up, but it does not deal with the likely cause. The first action is to remove the hepatotoxin.
B. Glucocorticoids: no role in drug-induced transaminitis. They would be used for autoimmune hepatitis or an RA flare, and she has neither.
D. Liver biopsy: kept for persistent abnormalities after stopping the drug, or suspected fibrosis. It is not the first step.
key_concept:
Methotrexate LFT rules work by multiples of the upper limit of normal (ULN).
  • Raised but <3x ULN: reduce the dose and repeat LFTs
  • >3x ULN: stop (withhold) methotrexate
  • Monitoring: LFTs, CBC and creatinine at regular intervals
  • Give folic acid with methotrexate
  • Avoid alcohol
exam_pearl: Above 3 times the upper limit, stop the drug first. Imaging and biopsy come only if the LFTs do not settle.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with asthma has not had a severe attack for the last 3 months. However, she has a history of cough and wheezing 2-3 times each week. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: cough and wheezing 2-3 times each week
why_right: Symptoms "2-3 times each week" with no severe attack means more than intermittent, i.e. mild persistent asthma. The step up from as needed reliever alone is a daily controller, and the core controller is a low dose inhaled corticosteroid, which treats the airway inflammation rather than just the bronchospasm.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ipratropium bromide is a short acting antimuscarinic; it is the key bronchodilator in COPD and only an add on in acute severe asthma, not a maintenance controller.
C. Salbutamol (SABA) is the reliever; alone it fits only intermittent symptoms. Symptoms several times a week need a controller added.
D. Salmeterol (LABA) must never be used as monotherapy in asthma (risk of fatal attacks); it is added to an ICS at higher steps when ICS alone fails.
key_concept:
Asthma stepping: frequency of symptoms decides the step; persistent symptoms need an anti-inflammatory controller.
  • Intermittent (rare symptoms): as needed reliever; GINA now prefers as needed low dose ICS-formoterol over SABA alone
  • Mild persistent: low dose ICS
  • Not controlled on ICS: add LABA (ICS/LABA combination)
  • LABA never alone in asthma
  • Ipratropium: COPD first line; add on in acute asthma
exam_pearl: Weekly daytime symptoms = persistent = ICS; a lone SABA or lone LABA is the trap.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with nausea, vomiting, and muscle aches. She is 6 days postoperative and is unable to pass stool, with abdominal distension. Laboratory results show hypokalemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Post-op day 6 with nausea, vomiting, muscle aches, inability to pass stool and abdominal distension is hypokalemia causing ileus. The danger in hypokalemia is cardiac arrhythmia, so the next step is an ECG to look for flattened T waves, U waves, ST depression and QT/QU prolongation before working out the cause; replacement proceeds alongside.
why_wrong_block:
B. Urine potassium separates renal from extrarenal loss; it belongs to the cause workup, done after cardiac risk is assessed.
C. Stool potassium is not a routine or urgent test and does not change immediate management.
D. Urine osmolality is part of the hyponatremia and polyuria workup, not hypokalemia.
key_concept:
Electrolyte emergency rule: assess the heart first (ECG), treat, then find the cause.
  • Hypokalemia features: weakness, cramps, ileus with distension, constipation, arrhythmia
  • ECG: flat T, U wave, ST depression, long QT/QU
  • Post-op ileus that persists: check potassium
  • Cause workup later: urine K (renal vs GI loss)
exam_pearl: "Next step" in a symptomatic potassium disorder is the ECG, not the cause hunting urine test.

stem: A patient with hepatorenal syndrome presents with low serum albumin and hyponatremia. What is the most likely type of hyponatremia in this patient?
why_right: Hepatorenal syndrome occurs on a background of decompensated cirrhosis: the fuller recall describes ascites, lower limb edema and a distended jugular vein with sodium 111 and low albumin. Total body water and sodium are both increased (water more than sodium) because of low effective arterial volume and ADH/RAAS activation, so this is hypervolemic hyponatremia, the type seen in cirrhosis, heart failure and nephrotic syndrome.
why_wrong_block:
A. Euvolemic hyponatremia (e.g. SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency) has no edema or ascites; this patient is clearly fluid overloaded.
C. Hypovolemic hyponatremia shows dehydration (vomiting, diarrhea, diuretics, dry mucosa, low JVP); edema, ascites and a raised JVP argue against it.
D. Pseudohyponatremia has normal serum osmolality from very high lipids or proteins; low albumin does not cause it, and true dilution is present here.
key_concept:
Classify hyponatremia by serum osmolality, then volume status.
  • Normal osmolality: pseudohyponatremia (lipids, proteins)
  • High osmolality: hyperglycemia, mannitol
  • Low osmolality + hypovolemic: GI loss, diuretics
  • Low osmolality + euvolemic: SIADH, hypothyroid, adrenal insufficiency
  • Low osmolality + hypervolemic: cirrhosis, heart failure, nephrotic, renal failure
  • Hypervolemic treatment: fluid restriction plus loop diuretic
exam_pearl: Edema or ascites with low sodium = hypervolemic; do not let "low albumin" pull you toward pseudohyponatremia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Fuller recall in this block: hepatorenal syndrome (not directly mentioned) with hepatomegaly, ascites, lower limb edema, distended jugular vein; Sodium 111 (low), low albumin. Same options; B highlighted.

stem: An 80-year-old man with known heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and atrial fibrillation presents with palpitations for 3 months. He denies shortness of breath, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, or chest pain. Vital signs : BP: 110/70 mmHg HR: 130 bpm RR: 18/min O₂ saturation: 95% Temperature: 36.6°C Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
highlight_terms_source: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
why_right: Known HFrEF with AF and HR 130 needs rate control, but the BP is only 110/70 in an 80-year-old. Digoxin slows AV conduction without negative inotropy (it is mildly positively inotropic), so it controls rate without worsening the failing ventricle or dropping the pressure; this is the classic choice for AF coexisting with heart failure.
why_wrong_block:
B. Diltiazem is a negatively inotropic non-dihydropyridine CCB and is avoided in HFrEF; it is a rate control choice in AF with preserved EF or no heart failure.
C. Ivabradine acts on the sinus node If current and needs sinus rhythm; it has no rate effect in AF (used in HFrEF in sinus rhythm with HR still high on a beta blocker).
D. Propranolol is a non-selective beta blocker not among HF-proven agents and can worsen failure and hypotension; in stable HFrEF the beta blockers used are bisoprolol, carvedilol or metoprolol succinate.
key_concept:
AF rate control is chosen by the ventricle and the BP.
  • AF + HFrEF or borderline BP: digoxin (or an HF beta blocker if stable)
  • AF without HF: beta blocker or diltiazem/verapamil
  • Avoid non-DHP CCB in HFrEF
  • Ivabradine: sinus rhythm only
  • Unstable AF: synchronized cardioversion
exam_pearl: Heart failure + fast AF in the exam key = digoxin; diltiazem is the trap.

stem: 43 yo gravid all normal abdomen soft lax, RT renal bruit during auscultation to confirm diagnosis
why_right: A renal bruit on auscultation points to renal artery stenosis (in a younger woman, fibromuscular dysplasia; in older smokers, atherosclerosis). The lead in asks to confirm the diagnosis, which needs vascular imaging of the renal arteries; the keyed "CT kidney" stands for CT angiography of the renal arteries, which shows the stenosis directly.
why_wrong_block:
B. Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler is a reasonable initial screening test for renal artery stenosis, but it is operator dependent and is not the confirmatory study; plain grey scale US only shows kidney size.
C. Plain abdominal radiography cannot show renal arteries or flow; it suits radiopaque stones or bowel gas patterns.
key_concept:
Renal artery stenosis: suspect, screen, then confirm with angiographic imaging.
  • Clues: abdominal or flank bruit, resistant or new onset HTN, AKI after ACEi/ARB, flash pulmonary edema
  • Young woman: fibromuscular dysplasia; older: atherosclerosis
  • Screening: duplex Doppler US
  • Confirm: CT angiography or MR angiography; catheter angiography is the gold standard
exam_pearl: "Confirm" pushes you from Doppler US to CT or MR angiography.

stem: 34-year-old woman a known case of SLE on hydroxychloroquine. She came to the clinic for routine checkup. She is asymptomatic with unremarkable clinical examination. Urine analysis and her blood test are done. She underwent renal biopsy, which revealed Class I (minimal change) lupus nephritis (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: Biopsy shows Class I (minimal mesangial) lupus nephritis in an asymptomatic patient already on hydroxychloroquine. Class I has an excellent renal prognosis and needs no kidney directed immunosuppression; management is supportive, with blood pressure control and monitoring while she continues hydroxychloroquine. Immunosuppression is reserved for the proliferative and membranous classes.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance: Class I is benign but it is still renal involvement; she needs BP control and regular urine and creatinine surveillance for transformation to a higher class, not reassurance alone.
B. Pulse steroid: induction with high dose or pulse steroids plus MMF or cyclophosphamide is for Class III/IV (and Class V with nephrotic range proteinuria), not minimal mesangial disease.
C. High-protein diet: increases glomerular hyperfiltration and is not advised in kidney disease; there is no indication here.
key_concept:
Lupus nephritis treatment follows the ISN/RPS class.
  • Class I (minimal mesangial): BP control
  • Class II (mesangial proliferative): supportive, ACE inhibitor for proteinuria
  • Class III/IV (focal/diffuse proliferative): steroid + MMF (or cyclophosphamide)
  • Class V (membranous): ACE inhibitor; add immunosuppression (e.g. MMF + steroid) if nephrotic range proteinuria
  • Class VI (advanced sclerosis): prepare for renal replacement
  • Hydroxychloroquine continues in all SLE
exam_pearl: Class I/II = supportive (BP control, ACE inhibitor for proteinuria); steroids plus MMF are for Class III/IV, and Class V only with nephrotic range proteinuria.

stem: patient with a history of HTN, DLP, CKD stage 3 on metformin, statin, and ACEI. He presents with SOB elevated JVP, and bilateral lower limb edema. On physical examination, a grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard. [ they provide CXR pic i think it was pulmonary edema but I'm not sure] Where should this patient be referred for counselling and further evaluation?
OptB: Endocrinologist for the use of metformin in CKD
OptC: Nephrologist for CKD and fluid balance
OptD: Cardiologist for evaluation of heart failure and valvular abnormalities
why_right: Shortness of breath, elevated JVP, bilateral leg edema, a likely pulmonary edema picture and a systolic murmur describe congestive heart failure with possible valvular disease in a hypertensive patient. The problem driving his presentation is cardiac, so he should go to a cardiologist for echocardiography, valve assessment and heart failure management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pulmonologist: pulmonary edema here is cardiogenic; a pulmonary referral fits primary lung disease (COPD, ILD, cor pulmonale workup).
B. Endocrinologist: metformin dosing in CKD stage 3 is a real issue but is handled by eGFR thresholds and is not the cause of edema, raised JVP and a murmur.
C. Nephrologist: CKD contributes to fluid retention, but CKD alone does not explain the murmur; fluid overload with a raised JVP and murmur in a hypertensive patient is primarily a cardiac question.
key_concept:
Refer to the specialty that owns the dominant new finding.
  • Raised JVP + edema + dyspnea: heart failure until proven otherwise
  • New murmur: echocardiography (TTE first)
  • HTN and CKD are risk factors for heart failure
  • Metformin in CKD: dose by eGFR, not a reason for this referral
exam_pearl: The murmur is the tie breaker: CKD explains edema, only the heart explains edema plus a murmur.

stem: Patient in his/her 20s in PE murmur increased with standing and diminished with handgrip. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A murmur that gets louder on standing and softer with handgrip in a young patient is mitral valve prolapse. Standing reduces preload, so the LV shrinks and the leaflets prolapse earlier (earlier click, longer murmur); handgrip raises afterload and LV size, delaying prolapse and shortening the murmur. Every other form of MR does the opposite with handgrip.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ischemic MR follows MI with papillary muscle dysfunction in an older patient; like other MR it gets louder with handgrip, not standing.
C. Functional MR comes from LV dilatation (dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failure); its murmur increases with handgrip and decreases with reduced preload.
D. Rheumatic MR is a holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla after rheumatic fever; like other fixed MR it gets louder with handgrip and softer, not louder, on standing.
key_concept:
Dynamic maneuvers: only MVP and HOCM get louder when preload falls.
  • Standing or Valsalva (less preload): MVP and HOCM louder, most others softer
  • Squatting or leg raise (more preload): MVP and HOCM softer
  • Handgrip (more afterload): MR, AR, VSD louder; MVP and HOCM softer; AS softer
  • MVP: mid-systolic click then late systolic murmur, young women
exam_pearl: Louder on standing and softer on handgrip = MVP or HOCM; a click or apex location picks MVP.

stem: Pt post renal transplant presented with gum hypertrophy (gingival hyperplasia). What is the cause?
why_right: A renal transplant recipient is on calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppression, and gingival hyperplasia is a classic side effect of cyclosporin A (tacrolimus, the alternative calcineurin inhibitor, rarely does it). Management is dental hygiene and switching to tacrolimus if troublesome.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vitamin D supplementation does not cause gum overgrowth; excess causes hypercalcemia. The vitamin linked to swollen, bleeding gums is vitamin C deficiency (scurvy).
C. Pantoprazole (PPI) is not associated with gingival hyperplasia; its side effects include hypomagnesemia, C. difficile and fractures.
key_concept:
Drug-induced gingival hyperplasia: three drug classes.
  • Cyclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor)
  • Phenytoin (anticonvulsant)
  • Calcium channel blockers, especially nifedipine
  • Cyclosporin also: nephrotoxicity, hypertension, hirsutism, hyperkalemia
  • Tacrolimus: nephrotoxicity and diabetes, little gum overgrowth or hirsutism
exam_pearl: Transplant + gum hypertrophy + hirsutism = cyclosporin; switching to tacrolimus is the fix.

stem: A 78-year-old woman presents with exertional syncope. On clinical examination, she has a slow rising carotid pulse and a loud ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge, radiating to the carotids. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
highlight_terms_source: ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge, radiating to the carotids
why_right: An elderly woman with exertional syncope, a slow rising carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the carotids has classic aortic stenosis. Syncope, angina and dyspnea are the symptom triad, and symptoms signal severe disease needing valve replacement.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mitral stenosis gives a mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap at the apex, typically post-rheumatic, presenting with dyspnea and AF, not a carotid radiating systolic murmur.
C. Mitral valve prolapse is a mid-systolic click with late systolic murmur at the apex in younger patients, not at the right upper sternal edge.
D. Tricuspid regurgitation is a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge that increases with inspiration, with raised JVP and prominent v waves.
key_concept:
Murmur location and radiation identify the valve.
  • AS: ejection systolic, right 2nd intercostal space, radiates to carotids, slow rising pulse
  • AS triad: syncope, angina, dyspnea (exertional)
  • MR: holosystolic apex, radiates to axilla
  • MS: mid-diastolic apex rumble with opening snap
  • TR: holosystolic left lower sternal edge, louder on inspiration
exam_pearl: Slow rising pulse + carotid radiation = aortic stenosis; HOCM also gives syncope but has a jerky pulse and no carotid radiation.

stem: Renal failure (stage 4?), bone pain, hyperparathyrodisim X-ray: metaphysel Fraying What will you see in the labs?
OptD: Eleveted 1,25 vit d (Elevated 100% sure but not sure regarding the vit d)
why_right: Advanced renal failure with bone pain, metaphyseal fraying and hyperparathyroidism is renal osteodystrophy. Long standing secondary hyperparathyroidism can become autonomous (tertiary hyperparathyroidism), and then calcium rises; among these options hypercalcemia is the only lab change that fits, since the others are the opposite of what CKD produces.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypokalemia: failing kidneys retain potassium, so CKD stage 4 tends toward hyperkalemia; hypokalemia fits GI or diuretic losses.
C. Hypophosphatemia: CKD causes phosphate retention, so phosphate is high; low phosphate is the pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism with normal kidneys.
D. Elevated 1,25 vitamin D: diseased kidneys cannot perform 1-alpha hydroxylation, so calcitriol is low in CKD; high calcitriol fits granulomatous disease or primary hyperparathyroidism.
key_concept:
Hyperparathyroidism lab patterns.
  • Primary: Ca high, PO4 low, PTH high
  • Secondary (CKD): Ca low or normal, PO4 high, PTH high, 1,25 vit D low
  • Tertiary (long standing CKD or post-transplant): Ca high, PTH very high; PO4 high in CKD, low or normal after transplant
  • CKD electrolytes: K high, PO4 high, metabolic acidosis
exam_pearl: Secondary HPT in CKD classically has low calcium; hypercalcemia means it has turned tertiary.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 3-month history of lower back pain associated with morning stiffness lasting almost 1 hour, as well as joint pain affecting both knees and ankles bilaterally. She denied any history of skin rash or mucosal ulcerations. No history of fever. Clinical examination reveals limited lumbar spine movements and active arthritis at both knees bilaterally. She also has tenderness over the Achilles tendon (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: lower back pain associated with morning stiffness
why_right: Low back pain for 3 months with morning stiffness of about 1 hour is inflammatory back pain. Add limited lumbar spine movement, a lower limb large joint peripheral arthritis (knees, ankles) and Achilles tenderness (enthesitis) and the picture is axial spondyloarthritis, i.e. ankylosing spondylitis. The absence of rash, mucosal ulcers and fever removes the main mimics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reactive arthritis needs a preceding GI or GU infection and often conjunctivitis or urethritis; none is described here, and it is usually an acute oligoarthritis rather than chronic axial disease.
B. Rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetric small joint polyarthritis (MCP, PIP, wrists) that spares the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints and does not typically cause Achilles enthesitis.
D. Crystal arthritis (gout, pseudogout) gives acute, episodic, very painful mono or oligoarthritis, not 3 months of inflammatory back pain with restricted lumbar movement.
key_concept:
Inflammatory back pain >3 months + enthesitis + limited lumbar motion = ankylosing spondylitis.
  • Inflammatory back pain: morning stiffness, better with activity, worse with rest, night pain
  • Peripheral: lower limb large joint arthritis (classically asymmetric oligoarthritis), Achilles enthesitis (heel pain)
  • Extra-articular: anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation, apical lung fibrosis
  • Diagnosis: sacroiliitis on imaging (MRI most sensitive early), HLA-B27
  • Treatment: NSAIDs first, then TNF inhibitors
exam_pearl: A woman does not exclude AS: chronic inflammatory back pain plus enthesitis is the key, not the sex.

stem: A 40-year-old man with paraplegia following road traffic accident one year ago is brought to the Emergency Department because of sudden onset dyspnea and chest pain. On examination, he is in severe distress and cyanosed. He has left parasternal heave and loud P2. Chest is clear to auscultation (see lab results and reports). Blood pressure 80/55 mmHg Heart rate 110/min Respiratory rate 30/min Temperature 36.6 °C Oxygen saturation 86 % Test Result Normal Values ABG HCO3- 22 22-28 mmol/L ABG PCO2 4.2 4.7-6.0 kPa pH 7.4 7.36-7.45 ABG PO2 8.6 10.6-14.2 kPa Echocardiogram: Dilated right ventricle with pulmonary artery pressure of 55 mmHg. Venous Doppler: Confirmed DVT in the left leg extending to the thigh. Which of the following is the best line of management?
why_right: Paraplegia means long-term immobilization, and the confirmed proximal DVT plus sudden dyspnea, chest pain, cyanosis and SpO2 86% make this acute pulmonary embolism. The decisive clue is BP 80/55 with HR 110: this is high-risk (massive) PE with shock, and right heart strain is confirmed by the parasternal heave, loud P2 and a dilated RV on echo. Unstable PE is treated with systemic thrombolysis, so an alteplase infusion is the best line of management.
why_wrong_block:
A. An IVC filter only stops new emboli and does nothing for the clot already obstructing the pulmonary circulation; it is used when anticoagulation is contraindicated or PE recurs despite adequate anticoagulation.
C. LMWH is the treatment for hemodynamically stable PE; with hypotension it is too slow to relieve the obstruction, so thrombolysis comes first (heparin follows).
D. Warfarin takes days to work and is long-term secondary prevention, never the acute treatment of PE with shock.
key_concept:
Acute PE: the blood pressure decides the treatment.
  • Hypotension or shock (massive PE): thrombolysis (alteplase)
  • Thrombolysis contraindicated or failed: surgical or catheter embolectomy
  • Stable PE: anticoagulation (LMWH or DOAC)
  • IVC filter: anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrence despite it
  • RV strain signs: parasternal heave, loud P2, dilated RV on echo
exam_pearl: The same PE with a normal blood pressure flips the answer to enoxaparin; hypotension is what makes it alteplase.

stem: A 62-year-old patient with a known case of chronic hepatitis C presented with abdominal pain and swelling. Examination showed ascites, abdominal tenderness and peripheral edema. Diagnostic ascitic tap done and revealed a neutrophil count of 400/mm (<250 mm) Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 90 /min Temperature 37.6 °C Which of the following is the appropriate next step in the management?
why_right: A cirrhotic patient (chronic hepatitis C) with ascites who develops abdominal pain and tenderness has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until proven otherwise. The diagnostic tap confirms it: ascitic neutrophils 400/mm3, above the 250 threshold, even though the fever is only low grade (37.6). SBP is treated with IV antibiotics, classically a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, started without waiting for culture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fluid restriction is part of routine ascites care (mainly for dilutional hyponatremia) and does not treat an infected peritoneum.
B. Spironolactone is the first-line diuretic for uncomplicated cirrhotic ascites; it would be the answer if the neutrophil count were below 250 with no infection.
D. Large-volume paracentesis is for tense or diuretic-refractory ascites; it does not treat SBP, which must be covered with antibiotics first.
key_concept:
Ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm3 = SBP = IV antibiotics.
  • Ascites with abdominal pain in cirrhosis: tap and treat as SBP
  • SBP first line: IV third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone)
  • Uncomplicated ascites: sodium restriction, then spironolactone, add furosemide
  • Tense or refractory ascites: therapeutic paracentesis
exam_pearl: SBP often has little or no fever; the neutrophil count, not the temperature, makes the diagnosis.

stem: Women had a wound from the garden and the nurse found that the pt had tetanus vaccine 12 years ago. What to do ?
why_right: A garden wound is soil-contaminated, so it counts as a tetanus-prone (dirty) wound. For a dirty wound a booster is due if the last tetanus dose was more than 5 years ago, and hers was 12 years ago, so she needs a booster now. An adult booster is given as Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis), which also refreshes pertussis protection; tetanus immunoglobulin is not needed when the primary series was completed.
why_wrong_block: A. "Tetanus shot" is vague: it does not specify the booster form, and a tetanus-only shot misses the diphtheria and pertussis protection that Tdap gives; it is also not tetanus immunoglobulin, which is only for unknown or incomplete vaccination with a dirty wound.
key_concept:
Tetanus wound prophylaxis depends on the wound type and the time since the last dose.
  • Clean minor wound: booster if last dose >10 years ago
  • Dirty or tetanus-prone wound: booster if last dose >5 years ago
  • Unknown or fewer than 3 doses: vaccine, plus TIG if the wound is dirty
  • Adult booster of choice: Tdap if not given before, otherwise Td or Tdap
exam_pearl: Do not apply the 10-year rule to a dirty wound; soil contamination drops the cutoff to 5 years.

stem: 28-year-old woman with active neuropsychiatric lupus based on clinical manifestations and her workups. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy?
why_right: Active neuropsychiatric lupus is organ- and life-threatening SLE, so it needs induction with high-dose corticosteroids plus an immunosuppressant. Cyclophosphamide is the preferred immunosuppressant for severe inflammatory neuropsychiatric lupus. The lead-in asks for first-line therapy, so the combination of corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide is the answer.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cyclophosphamide alone omits the high-dose corticosteroid that is part of first-line induction; the two are given together.
C. Rituximab is reserved for refractory disease that fails steroids and cyclophosphamide, not first line.
D. Steroids alone are not enough for life-threatening lupus; they would suit mild flares, while severe organ involvement needs an added immunosuppressant.
key_concept:
SLE treatment scales with organ threat.
  • All patients: hydroxychloroquine as the cornerstone
  • Mild (skin, joints): hydroxychloroquine with NSAID or low-dose steroid
  • Severe (neuropsychiatric, renal): high-dose steroid plus cyclophosphamide
  • Refractory: rituximab
exam_pearl: Pick the combination: in severe lupus, steroid alone and cyclophosphamide alone are both traps.

stem: 55-year-old obese non-smoker man with hypertension presents with exertional dyspnea for 2 years. His wife stated that he is uncomfortable while sleeping at night and produces loud snores. Examination revealed central cyanosis, suffused conjunctivae and clear chest. BMI 40 kg/m2 Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
why_right: An obese (BMI 40) man with loud snoring and disturbed sleep reported by his wife has obstructive sleep apnea until proven otherwise. Hypertension is a recognised complication, and central cyanosis with suffused conjunctivae (hypoxemia with secondary polycythemia) and a clear chest point to a sleep-related breathing problem, not a lung disease. Polysomnography (overnight sleep study) is the diagnostic test, so it has the highest diagnostic value here.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spirometry diagnoses obstructive lung disease such as asthma or COPD; this non-smoker has a clear chest and a sleep history, not airway disease.
B. Spiral CT (CT pulmonary angiography) is for suspected pulmonary embolism with sudden dyspnea; this is a 2-year picture with snoring.
D. Methacholine challenge confirms asthma when spirometry is normal but symptoms suggest it; there is no wheeze or trigger history here.
key_concept:
Snoring + obesity + daytime or night symptoms = OSA → polysomnography.
  • Clues: loud snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, obesity, hypertension
  • Diagnosis: polysomnography
  • Treatment: weight loss plus nasal CPAP
  • Cyanosis, plethora and hypercapnia suggest obesity hypoventilation overlap
exam_pearl: "Highest diagnostic value" for a snorer is the sleep study, not a lung test, even when dyspnea is the complaint.
